name: 18-evpn-leaf-spine
description:
A data-centre fabric: two **spines**, three **leaves**, and on each leaf one PC in **VLAN 10** and one in **VLAN 20**. The spines only route; the VLANs stretch across all three leaves through **VXLAN** tunnels, and **BGP EVPN** tells each leaf which MAC addresses are behind which other leaf. PCs in the same VLAN reach each other, wherever they are; PCs in different VLANs don't.

| | Address | AS |
|---|---|---|
| spine1, spine2 | `10.1.<leaf>.1`, `10.2.<leaf>.1` on the links to the leaves | 65000 |
| leaf1, leaf2, leaf3 | VTEP `10.255.0.11`, `.12`, `.13` (loopback); `10.1.<leaf>.2` to spine1, `10.2.<leaf>.2` to spine2 | 65001, 65002, 65003 |
| pc10-1, pc10-2, pc10-3 | `10.10.0.11`, `.12`, `.13` | VLAN 10, VNI 10010 |
| pc20-1, pc20-2, pc20-3 | `10.20.0.11`, `.12`, `.13` | VLAN 20, VNI 10020 |

On each leaf: `eth0` goes to spine1, `eth1` to spine2, `eth2` to its VLAN 10 PC and `eth3` to its VLAN 20 PC.

## What's already there
**Deploy**. Each leaf's startup commands build its **data plane** (click a leaf to read them): the VTEP address on its loopback, its uplink addresses, and for each VLAN a Linux bridge with the PC's port and a VXLAN interface (VNI 10010 or 10020) in it. Look at it in a leaf's console:
```
ip -br addr
bridge link
ip -d link show vxlan10
bridge fdb show dev vxlan10
```
What's missing is the **control plane**: no routing yet, so the leaves can't reach each other's VTEPs, and the VXLAN interfaces know no remote MAC addresses. `ping -c 2 10.10.0.13` from pc10-1 fails.

## Configure BGP: the underlay and EVPN
eBGP in two layers over the same sessions: **IPv4** carries the leaves' VTEP addresses (the *underlay*), and **L2VPN EVPN** carries MAC addresses and VNIs (the *overlay*). Open each node's **Console**, start `vtysh`, and type or paste its block.

**spine1**
```
configure terminal
router bgp 65000
 bgp router-id 10.255.0.1
 no bgp ebgp-requires-policy
 neighbor LEAVES peer-group
 neighbor LEAVES remote-as external
 neighbor 10.1.1.2 peer-group LEAVES
 neighbor 10.1.2.2 peer-group LEAVES
 neighbor 10.1.3.2 peer-group LEAVES
 address-family l2vpn evpn
  neighbor LEAVES activate
 exit-address-family
end
write memory
```
**spine2**
```
configure terminal
router bgp 65000
 bgp router-id 10.255.0.2
 no bgp ebgp-requires-policy
 neighbor LEAVES peer-group
 neighbor LEAVES remote-as external
 neighbor 10.2.1.2 peer-group LEAVES
 neighbor 10.2.2.2 peer-group LEAVES
 neighbor 10.2.3.2 peer-group LEAVES
 address-family l2vpn evpn
  neighbor LEAVES activate
 exit-address-family
end
write memory
```
**leaf1**
```
configure terminal
router bgp 65001
 bgp router-id 10.255.0.11
 no bgp ebgp-requires-policy
 neighbor SPINES peer-group
 neighbor SPINES remote-as external
 neighbor 10.1.1.1 peer-group SPINES
 neighbor 10.2.1.1 peer-group SPINES
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  network 10.255.0.11/32
 exit-address-family
 address-family l2vpn evpn
  neighbor SPINES activate
  advertise-all-vni
 exit-address-family
end
write memory
```
**leaf2**
```
configure terminal
router bgp 65002
 bgp router-id 10.255.0.12
 no bgp ebgp-requires-policy
 neighbor SPINES peer-group
 neighbor SPINES remote-as external
 neighbor 10.1.2.1 peer-group SPINES
 neighbor 10.2.2.1 peer-group SPINES
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  network 10.255.0.12/32
 exit-address-family
 address-family l2vpn evpn
  neighbor SPINES activate
  advertise-all-vni
 exit-address-family
end
write memory
```
**leaf3**
```
configure terminal
router bgp 65003
 bgp router-id 10.255.0.13
 no bgp ebgp-requires-policy
 neighbor SPINES peer-group
 neighbor SPINES remote-as external
 neighbor 10.1.3.1 peer-group SPINES
 neighbor 10.2.3.1 peer-group SPINES
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  network 10.255.0.13/32
 exit-address-family
 address-family l2vpn evpn
  neighbor SPINES activate
  advertise-all-vni
 exit-address-family
end
write memory
```

> [!NOTE]
> `advertise-all-vni` makes the leaf announce every VNI it has (its VXLAN interfaces), with the MAC addresses learned on their bridges. `remote-as external` accepts any AS other than the router's own, so the configuration doesn't list the neighbours' AS numbers. Both spines are AS 65000: a route that went through one spine is never accepted by the other, which prevents loops.

## Verify
1. On a leaf, in vtysh:
   ```
   show bgp summary
   show ip route bgp
   show evpn vni
   show bgp l2vpn evpn route type multicast
   ```
   Two spines *Established* for both address families, the two other VTEPs reachable **through both spines** (ECMP), both VNIs, and one *type 3* route per leaf and VNI: that's how leaves learn where to flood broadcasts such as ARP.
2. From **pc10-1**: `ping -c 3 10.10.0.13` (pc10-3, on leaf3) works. Then, on a leaf:
   ```
   show evpn mac vni 10010
   show bgp l2vpn evpn route type macip
   ```
   The PCs' MAC addresses, local or *remote* behind another VTEP: *type 2* routes. In the leaf's console (not vtysh), `bridge fdb show dev vxlan10` shows them installed on the VXLAN interface, with the remote VTEP as `dst`.
3. From **pc10-1**: `ping -c 2 10.20.0.12` (pc20-2, the other VLAN) fails.
4. Capture a **spine–leaf** cable while pc10-1 pings pc10-3: UDP port 4789 between two VTEP addresses, with the PCs' whole Ethernet frame and ping inside. Wireshark decodes the VXLAN header and its VNI.

## Go further
- [ ] **VLANs isolate, not subnets.** On pc20-1, move to VLAN 10's subnet: `ip addr flush dev eth0` then `ip addr add 10.10.0.21/24 dev eth0`. Can it reach pc10-2 now? Why not? (**Stop** and **Start** pc20-1 to restore it.)
- [ ] Stop **spine1** (click it, then Stop). Does pc10-1 still reach pc10-3? Look at `show ip route bgp` on leaf1. Start it again.
- [ ] Send a big packet from pc10-1: `ping -c 2 -s 1422 -M do 10.10.0.13` works, `-s 1423` doesn't. Where do those numbers come from? (Hint: the PCs' startup commands, and 1450 − 28.)

## Questions
- [ ] Why does the underlay only need to carry the leaves' loopback addresses, not the PCs' subnets?
- [ ] What would it take to let VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 talk to each other, and where would that routing happen?
- [ ] Why use BGP to learn MAC addresses, instead of flooding and learning as a classic switch does?

nodes.name: leaf1
nodes.startup:
# The data plane: this leaf's VTEP address, its uplinks, and per VLAN a bridge with a VXLAN tunnel.
# The control plane (FRR: BGP and EVPN) is yours to configure; see the lab description.
ip addr add 10.255.0.11/32 dev lo
ip addr add 10.1.1.2/30 dev eth0     # to spine1
ip addr add 10.2.1.2/30 dev eth1     # to spine2
for v in 10 20; do
  ip link add name br$v type bridge
  ip link add name vxlan$v type vxlan id 100$v local 10.255.0.11 dstport 4789 nolearning
  ip link set vxlan$v master br$v
  ip link set vxlan$v up
  ip link set br$v up
done
ip link set eth2 master br10       # pc10-1: VLAN 10
ip link set eth3 master br20       # pc20-1: VLAN 20

images.dockerlab/host:latest:
FROM alpine:latest

# Everyday tools for an end host: full ip, packet capture, DNS lookups, web requests
RUN apk add --no-cache iproute2 tcpdump bind-tools curl iputils
images.dockerlab/frr:latest:
FROM alpine:latest

# FRRouting (vtysh, zebra, staticd, ospfd, ripd, bgpd), plus the network tools
RUN apk add --no-cache frr iproute2 tcpdump bind-tools curl iputils

# Turn on the routing protocol daemons the labs use (zebra and staticd always run)
RUN sed -i -e 's/^ospfd=no/ospfd=yes/' -e 's/^ripd=no/ripd=yes/' -e 's/^bgpd=no/bgpd=yes/' /etc/frr/daemons

# Start FRR with the container; its configuration is /etc/frr/frr.conf (vtysh: write memory)
CMD ["sh", "-c", "/usr/lib/frr/frrinit.sh start; exec sleep infinity"]
